title: Mapping-space excision over a simplicial pushout along a monomorphism
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, products, Kan complexes, weak homotopy equivalences and internal functor simplicial sets of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and right fibrations of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations]. Let $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ be a degreewise monomorphism of small simplicial sets, let $f:A\to C$ be any simplicial map, and let $P=B\amalg_A C$ be their pushout in simplicial sets. Let $p:X\to P$ be any simplicial map and let $q:Y\to P$ be a right fibration. For $T\in\{A,B,C\}$ put $X_T=X\times_P T$ and $Y_T=Y\times_P T$. For maps $Z\to T$ and $W\to T$, define $M_T(Z,W)_n=\{Z\times\Delta^n\to W\text{ over }T\}$, with simplex operators by precomposition.

The canonical map $X_B\amalg_{X_A}X_C\to X$ is a simplicial isomorphism, and restriction is a simplicial isomorphism
$$M_P(X,Y)\xrightarrow{\cong}M_B(X_B,Y_B)\times_{M_A(X_A,Y_A)}M_C(X_C,Y_C).$$
All four mapping complexes are Kan and the restriction $M_B(X_B,Y_B)\to M_A(X_A,Y_A)$ is a Kan fibration. In particular the restriction map from $M_P(X,Y)$ to the path model of this pullback is a weak homotopy equivalence. Explicitly this path model is
$$M_B(X_B,Y_B)\times_{M_A(X_A,Y_A),\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,M_A(X_A,Y_A))\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,M_A(X_A,Y_A)}M_C(X_C,Y_C),$$
and the map inserts the constant path at the common restriction. Thus the restriction square of mapping complexes is homotopy Cartesian, with the homotopy pullback interpreted by [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison]. Neither $p$ nor the bases are assumed fibrant, $f$ need not be injective, and no slice model structure is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.3.11, final mapping-square argument, printed pp.84-85, and Lemma 2.2.3.4. The degreewise reconstruction is the explicit expansion previously inline in item Step 5. Reading copy HTT.pdf and HTT.txt retained in the sandbox; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Compute the pushout in degree $r$ as the quotient of $B_r\amalg C_r$ by $i(a)\sim f(a)$ for $a\in A_r$, using the colimit universal property of [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Because $i_r$ is injective, its classes have the following description: each $b\notin i_r(A_r)$ is a singleton class, and for each $c\in C_r$ there is one class consisting of $c$ and all $i_r(a)$ with $f_r(a)=c$. These classes partition the disjoint union and are exactly the equivalence relation generated by the displayed pairs. Thus $P_r$ is in bijection with $(B_r\setminus i_r(A_r))\amalg C_r$. For each $x\in X_r$, if $p(x)$ belongs to the first part there is a unique representative $(x,b)$ in $(X_B)_r$. If it belongs to the second part there is a unique representative $(x,c)$ in $(X_C)_r$; its other representatives are exactly $(x,i_r(a))$ for the $a$ mapping to $c$, and each is identified with $(x,c)$ by $(x,a)\in(X_A)_r$. Identifications never change $x$. Therefore the canonical map $(X_B)_r\amalg_{(X_A)_r}(X_C)_r\to X_r$ is bijective. The degreewise quotients carry the induced simplex operators, since the generating identifications commute with those operators. Their universal property degreewise is therefore the simplicial pushout property. The canonical map is simplicial and bijective in each degree, so its degreewise inverse is simplicial. This proves the first isomorphism, without requiring $f$ to be injective.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.3.11, final strict mapping-square argument; explicit degreewise reconstruction of its pushout.

proof.text: Fix a parameter simplex $\Delta^n$. The same reconstruction with the extra unchanged coordinate $t\in(\Delta^n)_r$ shows that $X\times\Delta^n$ is the pushout of $X_B\times\Delta^n$ and $X_C\times\Delta^n$ over $X_A\times\Delta^n$: every generating identification retains both $x$ and $t$. A map $X_T\times\Delta^n\to Y_T$ over $T$ is exactly a map to $Y$ over $P$ together with its already prescribed $T$ coordinate; the inverse sends $(x,t)$ to the pair consisting of its image in $Y$ and the $T$ coordinate of $x$. In particular this identification does not require $T\to P$ to be injective. A compatible pair of the $B$ and $C$ maps consequently glues uniquely to $X\times\Delta^n\to Y$ over $P$, by that pushout property. Its restriction recovers the pair, and gluing the restrictions of a global map recovers that map by uniqueness. Precomposition in $\Delta^n$ commutes with restriction and gluing, again by uniqueness. These inverse degreewise bijections therefore give precisely the stated isomorphism of mapping simplicial sets, including its canonical projections.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.3.11, final pullback square; explicit parameterwise gluing.

proof.text: For each $T\in\{A,B,C\}$, the projection $q_T:Y_T\to T$ is a right fibration. Indeed a positive-index horn in $Y_T$ over a specified simplex of $T$ projects to a horn in $Y$ over its composite simplex in $P$. Lift it using $q$, and pair that lift with the specified simplex of $T$. This solves exactly the original pullback lifting problem. Also $X_A\to X_B$ is degreewise injective: under $X_A\simeq X_B\times_B A$, it sends $(x,a)$ to $(x,i(a))$, so injectivity follows from injectivity of $i$ in that degree. The displayed identification retains the same $a$ coordinate and is inverse to this fiber product formula.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.3.4, pullback restriction setup; degreewise verification of the right-fibration and monomorphism hypotheses.

proof.text: For each $T\in\{P,A,B,C\}$ (with $X_P=X$, $Y_P=Y$, $q_P=q$), show $M_T(X_T,Y_T)\to\Delta^0$ is a right fibration. Fix a positive-index horn $H=\Lambda_k^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m$, $m\geq1$, $0<k\leq m$. A horn in this mapping complex is exactly a map $X_T\times H\to Y_T$ over $T$. Explicitly a parameter $v\in H_r$ gives the $r$-simplex of the mapping complex represented by $(x,\alpha:[s]\to[r])\mapsto h_s(x,H(\alpha)v)$; conversely evaluate a parameter family at $(x,\mathrm{id}_{[r]})$. These inverse rules commute with all simplex operators by the definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. The horn inclusion is right anodyne by [def-coef-infinity-right-anodyne]. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-right-anodyne-product] with this horn and the monomorphism $\varnothing\to X_T$: its pushout-product is $H\times X_T\to\Delta^m\times X_T$, up to exchanging factors. By [lem-coef-right-anodyne-lifting-characterization], the right fibration $q_T$ lifts against this map over the specified base map $(t,x)\mapsto p_T(x)$. Exchanging factors back and applying the inverse parameter rule produces a filler for the original horn in $M_T$. Thus all four projections to $\Delta^0$ are right fibrations.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.3.4, empty-source application of the right-anodyne pushout-product argument; compare Kerodon Proposition 4.2.5.3 (0153).

proof.text:
Now show $\rho:M_B(X_B,Y_B)\to M_A(X_A,Y_A)$ is a right fibration. A lifting problem for $\rho$ against a positive-index horn $H=\Lambda_k^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m$ gives a map $X_B\times H\to Y_B$ and a map $X_A\times\Delta^m\to Y_B$ over $B$, agreeing on $X_A\times H$. Here the second map is obtained from its prescribed map into $Y_A$ by projecting to $Y_B$; conversely its $A$ coordinate is already fixed by $X_A$. By the parameter formulas in Step 4 these descriptions are inverse. Glue the two maps to
$$(X_B\times H)\amalg_{X_A\times H}(X_A\times\Delta^m)\longrightarrow Y_B.$$
The map from its source to $X_B\times\Delta^m$ is the pushout-product of the horn with the monomorphism $X_A\to X_B$ of Step 3, with factors exchanged. It is right anodyne by [lem-coef-infinity-right-anodyne-product]. Apply [lem-coef-right-anodyne-lifting-characterization] to $q_B$, with base map the projection to $X_B$ followed by $X_B\to B$. The resulting extension transposes to the required simplex in $M_B$, with exactly the given horn and exactly the given restriction in $M_A$. This proves the right-fibration assertion for $\rho$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.3.4, first paragraph of proof, with its Corollary 2.1.2.7 input supplied by the existing right-anodyne product node.

proof.text: The point $\Delta^0$ is Kan: every horn has its unique map to it, extending uniquely to the simplex. Apply [lem-cbc-right-fibration-space-fiber] to each of the four right fibrations over $\Delta^0$ in Step 4. Its hypothesis permits arbitrary simplicial total spaces and empty fibers, and its conclusion says that each total space $M_T$ is Kan. Apply the same statement to the right fibration $\rho$ of Step 5, whose base $M_A$ is now Kan. It follows that $\rho$ lifts every horn, including the initial horns. Hence $\rho$ is the claimed Kan fibration. No claim that $P,A,B,C$, or $X_T$ is fibrant has entered the argument.

source.place: Corollary 4.4.3.8, right fibration over a Kan base; this is the final implication in HTT Lemma 2.2.3.4.

proof.text: Put $U=M_B(X_B,Y_B)$, $V=M_C(X_C,Y_C)$ and $W=M_A(X_A,Y_A)$, with maps $u=\rho$ and $v$ the other restriction. Step 6 gives three Kan complexes and a Kan fibration $u$. Thus [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison] applies: its path model is Kan and its constant-path insertion $U\times_W V\to P(u,v)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. The isomorphism in Step 2 identifies $M_P(X,Y)$ with $U\times_W V$ using these exact projections. Composing it with constant-path insertion is therefore exactly the comparison map stated in the item, rather than an unspecified equivalence with the same objects. This proves the asserted homotopy Cartesian property with the prescribed path model.
